Depression

In Barrett et al.'s responder-randomized trial, adding transcranial infrared stimulation to CBT reduced depressive symptoms more than sham. The ELATED-3 trial found no significant symptom advantage over sham. A wearable trial reported better sleep scores but no between-group difference in depressive symptoms.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In Barrett et al.'s responder-randomized trial, adding transcranial infrared stimulation to CBT reduced depressive symptoms more than sham. The ELATED-3 trial found no significant symptom advantage over sham. A wearable trial reported better sleep scores but no between-group difference in depressive symptoms.

Summary of the Evidence

The Brain > Depression category contains 50 unique titles: 19 human reports, 16 animal papers, and 15 reviews or meta-analyses. The human set includes 13 randomized trials, five non-randomized or observational reports, and one case report. One publication also has an in-vitro arm, so method counts overlap. Reviews summarize the primary papers and do not add patient cohorts. Two recent transcranial physiology papers may report overlapping participants and do not test symptom efficacy.

Human and clinical evidence

Results differ by treatment and population. In Barrett et al.'s trial, 60 people began internet CBT and 40 CBT responders were randomized to active or sham transcranial infrared stimulation. Adding active light produced further depressive symptom reduction after four weekly sessions (2025). By contrast, the 54-person ELATED-3 sham-controlled trial found no significant difference in depressive symptoms after six weeks (Iosifescu et al. 2022). A 48-person wearable trial found no group difference in depression scores, although sleep quality improved in the active group (Guu et al. 2025). The 2026 meta-analysis combines small studies with different routes and populations, so its pooled estimate does not establish one standard treatment (Seok et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

Sixteen studies use rodent models, with eight rat and eight mouse papers. They investigate biological mechanisms and behavior rather than clinical recovery.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

One publication includes a cell experiment alongside animal work. It is not a separate clinical study, and the category contains no independent patient-derived ex-vivo evidence.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols include transcranial lasers, wearable near-infrared devices, and other light-based approaches, with single-session experiments and repeated treatment schedules. Wavelength is the light's color band and affects how far it may travel through tissue. These devices and schedules are not interchangeable, and no optimal clinical dose or schedule has been established.

Interpretation

The strongest direct signal applies to added symptom reduction after CBT in selected responders. The null ELATED-3 result and small, mixed studies make a general claim for light alone unwarranted. Larger independent trials should test remission, daily function, and persistence after treatment.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term symptom reduction when transcranial infrared stimulation is added to internet-based CBT in selected responders Very low for transcranial light alone as a general depression treatment or for durable remission
Publications and records50 unique titles (exact Brain > Depression)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One responder-enriched randomized trial found added symptom reduction with light plus CBT, while a larger sham-controlled trial of light alone was null. Other studies mix devices, populations, and physiological outcomes. Independent trials with prespecified symptom endpoints, adequate sample sizes, and longer follow-up are needed to judge remission and durability.
